source.title: Chain-of-Thought Hub: A Continuous Effort to Measure Large Language Models' Reasoning Performance
source.authors: Yao Fu; Litu Ou; Mingyu Chen; Yuhao Wan; Hao-Chun Peng; Tushar Khot

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream reasoning benchmark performance across language models of different parameter counts and reports a scale–performance relationship. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that benchmark performance generally correlates with model scale and approximately follows a log-linear trend (Figure 1). Table 1 also contains scores marked as the authors' tests, but most table results are attributed to other papers; the reported scores are not presented as fitted scaling laws. No results directly test held-out loss, extrapolation from small runs, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture-shape effects.
record.test_reason: The paper plots downstream reasoning accuracy against log parameter count (Figure 1) and reports an approximate log-linear trend. That bears on V6's scale-to-downstream part. It measures no pretraining loss, allocation, shape or fitting choice. The evidence is weak: most plotted scores are compiled from other papers, the models mix families and training types (base and SIFT), and no fit or prediction is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that reasoning performance correlates with model scale, roughly log-linearly. They also say closed models (GPT, Claude, PaLM) lead open ones, and that leading models are mostly RLHF-tuned. They add that LLaMA-65B is close to code-davinci-002 and could approach ChatGPT with SFT and RLHF.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses few-shot chain-of-thought prompting and downstream benchmark accuracy across existing models; it does not reproduce a pretraining-loss scaling-law measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that models without disclosed scale generally perform better than models that disclose scale, but do not report a separate controlled analysis of this difference.
record.problems: The scale relationship is described qualitatively and shown in a figure, with no numerical fit or uncertainty reported. Models span different families and training types; many table results are taken from prior work, and the text notes that some non-public models are untested on some datasets.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 contains many benchmark scores, most attributed to prior work; they are not separate results of a fitted scale relationship. The authors' starred test scores are not extracted as individual rows because the table does not present them as scaling-law fits and the flattened layout does not consistently identify all model–metric assignments.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss is measured.
All: no fitted law is extrapolated to larger runs.
All: no compute-optimal allocation is studied.
All: no other modality or training regime is analysed for power-law form.
Predictability from pretraining loss; any quantitative fit or forecast of downstream accuracy; within-family controlled scaling.
All: no fitting-choice or curve-bending analysis.

record.verdict_notes: This is an evaluation and leaderboard compilation; the scale analysis is a side observation. Only a few starred Table 1 scores come from the authors' own tests, and most points in Figure 1 are cited results. The authors attribute much of the performance gap to RLHF and closed-source status rather than scale alone. This suggests scale by itself does not predict performance across families, but they do not quantify it. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations at fixed compute, including their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study reports an approximate relationship between model scale and downstream benchmark performance, but does not fit or validate predictions from pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and bending of curves away from a single power law.

rows.subject: models evaluated in Chain-of-Thought Hub (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Model scale measured in billion parameters; individual sizes not specified for this aggregate result.
rows.operation_detail: Compared model performance with log model scale across the evaluated models.
rows.measure: Relationship between downstream benchmark performance and log parameter count
rows.locator: Figure 1; section “Correlation between model scale and reasoning”
rows.note: The text characterizes the overall relationship as a general correlation with an approximate log-linear trend. No numerical fit, exponent, or prediction error is reported.
rows.check: Mostly correct. Most plotted values are taken from other papers (PaLM, Minerva, Flan, LLaMA reports), not measured here. The plot covers only models with disclosed sizes, across mixed families and training types. No fit, exponent or prediction error is given, so 'predictably' is shown only qualitatively ('approximately a log-linear trend'). Partial is kept for that reason.

relationships.condition: Models with disclosed parameter counts plotted in Figure 1 (PaLM, Minerva, Flan-PaLM, LLaMA, Flan-T5), few-shot CoT reasoning benchmarks
relationships.reason: The authors report reasoning accuracy is generally correlated with scale, roughly log-linear (r1). This is qualitative only, with no fit, and the scores are largely compiled from other papers.
relationships.display_finding: Reasoning accuracy generally increased roughly log-linearly with scale in scores largely compiled from other studies, without a fitted relationship.
